subject: Architecture
title: Building Codes: Written in Blood
description: Learn Building Codes: Written in Blood in one minute.

hook.text: Every line in a building code exists because someone was hurt or killed. Codes are written in blood.

buildup.text: The 1666 Great Fire of London led to stone-and-brick requirements. The 1871 Chicago fire created fireproofing codes.

discovery.text: The 1911 Triangle Shirtwaist fire — 146 workers died behind locked doors — created fire escape requirements.

twist.text: After 9/11, stairwell widths were increased and fireproofing standards were strengthened for tall buildings.

climax.text: Modern codes cover fire, earthquakes, wind, accessibility, and energy — thousands of pages of hard-won safety.

punchline.text: A boring document that saves millions. Every rule has a story.

quiz.question: What event led to mandatory fire escape requirements?
options: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire

details.summary: Building codes evolve through tragedy. The Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire, Iroquois Theatre fire, and countless collapses wrote their lessons into the regulations that protect us today.
details.whyItMatters: Building codes are invisible until they're violated. Understanding that each regulation represents a past disaster helps explain why code compliance isn't bureaucratic nuisance — it's the accumulated knowledge of catastrophic failures distilled into.
takeaways: Building codes are shaped by past tragedies and disasters
Fire exits, sprinklers, and occupancy limits all trace to deaths
Code compliance represents centuries of accumulated safety knowledge

faq.question: What disasters most shaped modern building codes?
faq.answer: The 1911 Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire (fire exits and sprinklers), 1903 Iroquois Theatre fire (outward-opening doors), 1942 Cocoanut Grove nightclub fire (occupancy limits), and the 9/11 attacks (wider stairways in high-rises). Each tragedy wrote new rules in blood.

faq.question: Are building codes the same everywhere?
faq.answer: No. Codes vary by country, state, and city, though most developed nations base theirs on international standards. Earthquake zones require seismic design, hurricane zones mandate wind resistance, and flood zones enforce elevation requirements. The level of enforcement also varies dramatically.
